name: Conditionals
moduleIntroduction: Welcome to the Conditionals module! This is the grammar of 'What If'. In French, you say 'Si je viens' or 'Si je viendrai'. In English, we have strict rules. The biggest rule? You almost never put 'Will' or 'Would' in the same part of the sentence as 'If'.
contrastiveExplanation:
First Conditional (Real Future):
English: If + Present, ... Will.
French: Often uses Future logic in both parts.

Second Conditional (Imaginary):
English: If + Past Simple, ... Would. (Use 'Were' for I/He/She).
French: Uses Imparfait (Si j'avais).

Third Conditional (Regret):
English: If + Past Perfect, ... Would Have.
French: Si j'avais su...

commonErrors.wrong: If I will see him, I will tell him.
commonErrors.correct: If I see him, I will tell him.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: Applying future logic to the 'if' clause. Never use 'will' after 'if'.

commonErrors.wrong: If I would have money, I would buy a car.
commonErrors.correct: If I had money, I would buy a car.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: Common error even in French ('Si j'aurais'). Never use 'would' in the 'if' clause.

commonErrors.wrong: If I was you, I would accept.
commonErrors.correct: If I were you, I would accept.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: Standard English uses the Subjunctive 'Were' for all persons in unreal situations.

commonErrors.wrong: Unless you don't study, you will fail.
commonErrors.correct: Unless you study, you will fail.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: French 'A moins que... ne...'. 'Unless' implies 'if not', so adding 'don't' creates a double negative.

commonErrors.wrong: If I knew, I would have come.
commonErrors.correct: If I had known, I would have come.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: Confusing Past Simple (Knew) with Past Perfect (Had known) for past regrets.

items.questionText: If you ___ water, it boils.

items.questionText: ___ he arrived earlier, he would have met her.
If I ___ known, I would not have come.
___ it not for your help, I would have failed.
items.feedback: Correct! 'Had it not been for' (Inverted Third Conditional). Wait, options are If, Had, Were. 'Were it not for' is Second Conditional. 'Had it not been for' is Third. The result is 'would have failed' (Third). So we need 'Had'. But the text says '___ it not for'. If it's 'Had', it must be 'Had it not BEEN for'. If it's 'Were', it's 'Were it not for'. 'Were it not for' implies present/general. 'I would have failed' is past. So it should be 'Had it not been'. Let's check if 'been' is in the text. No. '___ it not for your help'. This phrasing usually fits 'Were it not for' (Formal 2nd). But the result is 3rd. This is a mixed conditional or a slight error in the question text if strictly 3rd. However, 'Had it not for' is wrong. 'If it not for' is wrong. 'Were it not for' is the only grammatical chunk, even if tense is mixed. OR, maybe 'Had' implies 'Had it not [been] for'? No. Actually, 'Were it not for' can sometimes be used in mixed contexts, or the question meant 'Had it not BEEN'. Let's assume 'Were' is the intended structure for 'Without', or check if I can change the question to 'Had it not been'. I will assume 'Were' is the distractor and 'Had' is the target but missing 'been'. OR 'Were it not for' is correct for the idiom. Let's look at the answer key. It says 'Were'. 'Were it not for your help, I would have failed'. This is technically mixed (If it weren't for your help [fact], I would have failed [past]). This is valid.

frenchComparison.englishStructure: Were it not for your help...
